text.p: Celebrations after a moderate Moslem clergyman was elected president of Iran were subdued and security forces ensured nobody took the result as a signal to relax strict Islamic codes of dress and behaviour.
Hours after Saturday's announcement of the shock landslide victory by Mohammad Khatami, police mounted a high-profile presence on major Tehran highways and intersections to deter any boisterousness.
As dusk fell, special Guidance Patrols stopped cars to enforce Islamic dress codes. At least one woman was seen being rebuked by a female officer for wearing make-up.
By and large, the mostly youthful army of Khatami backers who worked for his election in hopes of economic and social reform stayed at home after the result.
Polling day on Friday fell in the middle of Muharram, the month of mourning observed as a time of grief and sorrow by Shi'ite Moslems.
The scale of Khatami's victory stunned the Islamic republic's clerical establishment.

He won 69 percent of the 29.1 million votes cast while his more widely known rival, conservative parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri who had been tipped to capture the presidency after a fierce campaign, got only 25 percent.
The turnout -- 29.1 million or 88 percent of the 33 million eligible voters -- was the largest in any Iranian election.

Khatami, 54, a senior clergyman's son and a former culture and Islamic guidance minister, is considered an open-minded religious intellectual and tolerant politician. He advocates more personal freedom, democracy and the rule of law.
The election turned into a referendum on the 18 years of revolution since fundamentalist Shi'ites toppled Iran's pro- American monarch, the Shah, in 1979.
In Washington, a State Department official said the United States would closely watch the election's aftermath to see whether there were real changes in Iran's behaviour.
The Clinton administration, accusing Iran's leaders of sponsoring "terrorism" abroad and seeking to acquire weapons of mass destruction, enforces a trade embargo aimed at isolating Tehran.
Tehran denies involvement in such action and says its arms build-up is defensive.
Khatami is due to take over in August when President Akbar Hashemi Rafsajani steps down after completing the maximum two four-year terms permitted by law.

Rafsanjani, 62, will remain an influential political figure in Iran's multi-layered government as head of a council which mediates any dispute between parliament and another body of clerics and lawyers.
